# AGENT.md: make this person's changelog site and its film You are a coding agent working for one person who ships things (a developer, an indie hacker, an engineer, a designer who codes). They picked this format: their site is **their release notes**. It opens on **Now** (what they're doing this month, dated), then their life as a changelog read top to bottom, newest first: a release per year (`v5 · 2026`), each entry tagged **Shipped / Joined / Moved / Learned / Wrote**. Shipped entries carry a small film of the thing working (the CLI's first run, the library's page, the app) that plays as it reaches the middle of the screen. A rail of contribution strips (one row per release, one cell per week, the entries marked on it) follows the scroll. It ends on **Unreleased**: a cursor drafts the next entry ("Working with you on …"), releases it, and their address appears. The same page opened with `?record` reads itself top to bottom: the film they post. The page only works if everything on it is **theirs and true**: their real projects, their real dates, their real words. You are assembling a record, not writing a persona. Never invent a project, an employer, a client, a date, a number (stars, downloads, users), a quote or a credential. If something is missing, leave the placeholder and ask. Read `tour/README.md` once for the engine's vocabulary (the parts that matter here: `type`, `stream`, `click`, `zoom`, `data-tour-frame`, *A third for squarish stages*, the `manual` driver, `recordStage`). Then work through this in order. ## 0. Where things are ``` index.html the page. Its markup is yours to edit: the top line, the log (
: the rail, Now, the releases, Unreleased), the footer kit/ placeholder kit: tokens, .ph frames, buttons, notes (press N to hide notes) changelog/section.css the page in its three layouts (.is-wide / .is-mid / .is-narrow), the films' products (.clt terminal, .clr project page, .cla app, .cln the Unreleased entry) changelog/script.js the films, one per data-film="…", and NEXT_LINE (the line the cursor drafts) changelog/section.js builds the rail, plays each film as it reaches the middle, and the ?record reading changelog/section.html the markup as it came (index.html has a filled-in copy; edit index.html) tour/ the engine (tour.js, tour.css), snapshot.py, README.md; don't edit ``` (In the StyleFeatures repo, `python3 templates/scaffolds/sections/demo/tour/export.py --format changelog` makes this layout.) Serve the folder with any static server, e.g. `python3 -m http.server 8000`. ## 1. Gather their things (before writing anything) Ask the person for what you can't find, and confirm anything you found before it goes public. Look in this order: - **GitHub** (`gh api users/`, `gh repo list --source --limit 100`, `gh release list -R `): their pinned repos, the ones with real releases, each repo's README first line, its install command, its first release date and its `v1.0.0` (or first stable) release notes. Pinned + released + described is a good filter for Shipped. - **Package registries**: npm (`npm view time --json` gives the first publish date), PyPI, crates.io, Homebrew, the App Store / Play Store page, a Chrome Web Store page. These give honest Shipped dates. - **Their CV or LinkedIn export** (`Positions.csv`, `Education.csv`): Joined, Moved and Learned entries with month and year. Use the role and team as they write them. - **Their writing**: blog RSS/Atom feed, Substack, dev.to, a `posts/` folder; talk recordings (YouTube/Vimeo) and the event page. These are Wrote entries: title as published, where, the month. - **A /now page** if they have one; otherwise ask them the four Now lines directly (Building, Learning, Reading, Based in). Now is present tense and true **this month**. - **Their contribution history**, if they want the strips filled: `gh api graphql` with `contributionsCollection(from:, to:) { contributionCalendar { weeks { contributionDays { contributionCount } } } }` per year, or `git log --author= --date=short --format=%ad` across their repos. Turn each year into 52 weekly levels 0–4 (quartiles of that person's own weeks, never compared with anyone else). If they'd rather not show it, leave the strips empty: the entries are still marked on them. - **Their look.** If they have a site, take its fonts and its one accent colour (`--cl-accent` and `--cl-accent-soft` on `.demo-changelog`). Otherwise keep the kit's warm paper, near-black ink and the quiet green. Then ask them: which years get a release (skip quiet ones: a gap in a log is honest), how they number versions (the default is one major per release, `v0.1` for where it starts; years-as-versions `v2026` also works), which three Shipped entries get a film, and the one line they want the Unreleased entry to say. ## 2. Fill Now and the log - **Top line** `.cl-top`: their name exactly as they write it, links to GitHub, the feed, and `#next`. - **Now** `.cl-now`: the date (`Updated November 2026`, and `datetime="2026-11"`), one sentence in `.cl-now-line` (one `` word at most), the four rows. Every time a line changes, the date changes. - **Releases** `.cl-release`, newest first. Each has `id` (`v5`), `data-year`, `data-version`, optionally `data-weeks="0,1,0,3,…"` (52 levels), a `

` with `.cl-v` and `.cl-y`, and one line for the year. - **Entries** `.cl-entry` with `data-tag` (`shipped|joined|moved|learned|wrote`) and `data-date="2025-10"` (or `2025-10-14`): the rail places the entry on its week from this, so it must be the real date. Inside: the month in `.cl-date`, the tag word, an `

` (the name, then `` the one-line what), one sentence of what changed, and `.cl-meta` links (repo, release notes, post, recording). Real links only; delete a link rather than point it at `#`. - A Shipped entry without a film gets a still: replace `.cl-still`'s `.ph` with `` (16:9). - The last release (`.cl-release-first`) is where it starts: "Initial commit" is a good title if it's true. - The footer, the `` ("Name: changelog") and the meta description (their Now line). - **The feed.** Generate `feed.xml` (Atom) from the entries (one `<entry>` per log entry, newest first, `updated` from `data-date`) so "Follow the log" is real. Regenerate it whenever the log changes. ## 3. Rebuild the three films (the Shipped entries' screens) Each film is a `.cl-film` inside its entry: a window (`data-tour-window`) with `data-size="720x450"` for wide and medium screens and `data-size-square="440x440"` for phones and 9:16 recordings (the film's stage is square there, so the window's product re-lays itself under `.is-square`). Its script is `films.<data-film>` in `changelog/script.js`. - **A CLI** (`data-film="cli"`, `data-chrome="terminal"`): the exact command from their README in `type('@cmd-1', …)`, then their tool's **real output**, line for line (run it in a scratch directory; `templates/scaffolds/sections/demo/terminal/ansi.py` in the StyleFeatures repo turns a captured run into HTML with colours). Keep it to what fits: one command, its output, one result. - **A library or project page** (`data-film="repo"`, `data-chrome="browser"`): their project as **their own docs or project site** shows it (not a copy of a code host's UI): name, README first line, the real install line in `.clr-install` (the Copy click), and the real notes of their first stable release in `.clr-notes` (Added / Changed / Fixed, as they wrote them). `data-url` is the address people would see. - **An app** (`data-film="app"`, `data-chrome="app"` or `browser` for a web app): harvest the real screen (`uv run tour/snapshot.py <url> --selector … --size 720x412 --out changelog/fragments/app.html --hook …`) or rebuild it from their view code in their tokens, then make the film do the one thing it's for: a new item, then its page. `ITEM` in `script.js` is that item's name, in the app's own vocabulary. - Other shipped things fit the same slots: a site (`browser`), a phone app (`data-chrome="phone"` with `data-size="390x844"` and a matching stage aspect), a design system's docs page, a dataset's explorer. - **Static HTML/CSS only, no app logic.** Their sample content or kit placeholders where user data would appear; never real people's data. - **Pace**: 7–11 s each, every click visibly changes something, one push-in at most (`zoom('@x', 1.3)`) then `unzoom()`, and the last frame is the result. Set `still` to that result (shown with reduced motion). ## 4. The rail and the reading You don't write the rail: `section.js` builds a row per release from the markup. Check it after filling the log: every entry is a mark on its week (Shipped in the accent), the head moves to the entry at the reading line, clicking a mark goes to its entry. On phones and tablets it's a bar across the top that shows the release being read. ## 5. Unreleased: the ending - `NEXT_LINE` in `changelog/script.js` is the line the cursor drafts: what they want to do next, with the visitor, in their own words, one line ("Working with you on …"). `next_version` in `.cln-t1` is the version it becomes. - `.cl-addr`: the email they want strangers to use, set large; GitHub; the feed; their domain. - `.cln-sub` is the second line of the draft. Keep it short and true. ## 6. Check it - The page at 1440 × 900 and on a 390-wide phone: each film plays once as it reaches the middle and shows "Play again" after; the rail follows; no sideways scroll; the Unreleased entry drafts and the address appears. - `index.html?t=6` freezes every film at 6 s. With reduced motion every film shows its `still` and the address is in. - `?record&ratio=16:9`, `ratio=1:1` and `ratio=9:16`, each with several `&t=` (`window.changelog.duration` is the length; `changelog.seek(30)` jumps there): the reading holds on Now, stops at each release, plays each film with its entry above it, and ends on Unreleased with the address in. Text must be readable in 1:1. - Nothing left that is lorem, a placeholder you meant to replace, a link to `#`, a number you can't source, or contact details they didn't agree to publish. Delete every `<span class="sf-note">`. ## 7. Hand it over: record and post End by giving the person this, with the link filled in: 1. Open **`index.html?record&ratio=16:9`** (served, e.g. `http://localhost:8000/?record&ratio=16:9`) in a browser window 1920 × 1080 if your screen allows, otherwise the largest 16:9 window you can make on a Retina display. 2. Record it with **Monet Shot**: choose the browser window, crop to the stage, park the real pointer off the window (the films draw their own cursor). It holds on Now for 1.2 s, reads the whole log once by itself and stops on the Unreleased entry with the address in. Monet Shot adds no zooms of its own, because the clicks aren't real clicks; if you'd rather place zooms on its timeline, open `?record&ratio=16:9&camera=off` so you don't get both. 3. Export H.264 MP4 and post it to X with one line and the link. **16:9** is for X and LinkedIn; `ratio=1:1` for the feed; `ratio=9:16` for stories and reels. Record each ratio separately; the page lays itself out again for each, so never crop one into another. 4. X takes MP4 (H.264, AAC) up to 2 min 20 s and 512 MB. There's no caption line: the log's own entries are set large enough to read muted, so keep the entry text short. 5. When something ships, add the entry, change Now's date, regenerate `feed.xml`, and record again: the changelog is meant to be kept. ## The painting it sits on Opened on its own, the page sits on *Mont Sainte-Victoire and Château Noir* by Paul Cézanne (public domain), the way Monet Shot frames a take: the site is a sheet with rounded corners and the painting fills the margin. It lives in `backdrop/` (`painting.webp` and a small `backdrop.js`). It turns itself off with `?record` (Monet Shot adds its own painting), with `?bare`, and inside a frame. Keep it, swap `painting.webp` for another, or delete the `backdrop.js` script line in `index.html` to drop it. ## When it's done: record your launch video with Monet Shot [Monet Shot](https://monetshot.pages.dev/) is a free screen recorder, made for pages like this one: it frames every take on a painting and zooms where things happen. Download it for [Mac](https://github.com/SocialAcolyte/monet-shot/releases/download/v0.1.1/MonetShot-0.1.1.zip), [Windows](https://github.com/SocialAcolyte/monet-shot/releases/download/desktop-v0.1.1/MonetShot-0.1.1-windows-x64-setup.exe) or [Linux](https://github.com/SocialAcolyte/monet-shot/releases/download/desktop-v0.1.1/MonetShot-0.1.1-x86_64.AppImage) (Windows and Linux are test builds; other packages are on the [releases page](https://github.com/SocialAcolyte/monet-shot/releases)). 1. Open the finished site with `index.html?record&ratio=16:9&captions=on` (use `ratio=1:1` or `ratio=9:16` for square and vertical posts). Only the stage shows, it plays once from the start, and captions are on, because X autoplays muted. 2. In Monet Shot, pick the browser window, crop to the stage, and park your real pointer off it (the tour draws its own cursor). Record one play-through. 3. Export, and post it with a link to the site. **For the agent:** when the site is finished, end your last message to the person with this step: the full `index.html?record&ratio=16:9&captions=on` link on their real URL (and the 1:1 and 9:16 versions), and the Monet Shot download link above for their computer.

# tour.js: the demo-film engine One engine for every StyleFeatures demo film. A template supplies a window with a product inside it and a script; the engine plays it with a fake cursor, a camera, chapter cards and captions, and drives it from a scroll, a clock, a screen recorder or a frozen `?t=`. Files: | file | what it is | edit it? | |---|---|---| | `tour.js` | the engine: step builders, `Tour`, `include()` | no, it's shared by every format | | `tour.css` | the engine's look: chromes, cursor, card, caption, keys, controls, record stage | no; restyle through its tokens | | `script.js` | this film's script | yes | | `section.html` / `section.css` | this film's band, closing frame and product | yes | | `snapshot.py` | harvests a live screen into a static fragment | no | | `export.py` | copies the whole format out as a standalone folder | no | | `AGENT.md` | the brief for the coding agent that fills it in | read it | Everything on screen is a pure function of one number, `t`, in seconds. Each frame the engine works out the product's state at `t` (classes, attributes, text, CSS variables, scroll positions), the camera, the cursor and the overlays, then writes only what changed. Nothing depends on what happened in earlier frames, so any moment renders on its own, the same way every time. ## Markup ```html
… your product, built at 1200 × 750 design pixels …
…
…
``` The engine adds the chrome, the cursor, ripples, the chapter card, the caption line, key caps, and the driver's controls. The opening band (`data-tour-band`) slides away in the first `intro` seconds; the closing frame (`data-tour-end`) gets `--in` 0→1 at the end and its own CSS decides what that looks like. The root also carries `--tour-band` (1 → 0 over the intro), `--tour-out` (0 → 1 over the outro) and `--tour-p` (0 → 1 over the whole film) for a format's own CSS. `data-tour-band="css"` stops the engine sliding the band away; the format fades or moves it from `--tour-band` instead. **A frame the format draws: `data-tour-frame`.** Put an element with `data-tour-frame` in the stage and lay it out in CSS (a phone's glass, a mat around a screenshot, a different box per ratio). The engine fits the window to it exactly, clips the camera to it (with its `border-radius`), and every zoom stays inside it: the window always covers the frame, so a push-in never shows what's around it. The outro then leaves the window where it is (use `--tour-out` to do something else). Give the frame the window's aspect ratio. `demo/phone` (the glass, beside the text or under it) and `demo/launch-note` (a mat on the page, a different box per recording ratio) use it. ### Window chromes: `data-chrome` | value | looks like | typical `data-size` | |---|---|---| | `browser` | traffic lights, back/forward, an address pill (`data-url`), share/new icons | `1200x750` | | `app` | a macOS title bar with traffic lights and a centred `data-title` | `1200x760` | | `phone` | a dark bezel, a status bar with the time and a notch | `390x844` | | `none` | just rounded corners | anything | | `terminal` | a warm charcoal window, traffic lights, a centred `data-title`; tokens `--tour-term-bg/-bar/-ink/-dim` | `780x548` | **Windows inside the window.** Any element inside the window with a `data-chrome` gets that chrome too, and a frame (`display:flex`, rounded, clipped). With `data-chrome="none"` on the outer window (made transparent in your CSS) it becomes a desk holding, say, a terminal and a browser; the camera pans between them with `zoom()` (`demo/terminal` does this). **A second design size for tall stages.** `data-size-tall="440x820"` on the window (or `sizeTall: [440, 820]` in the script) is used whenever the stage is taller than wide (W/H < .8: phones, 9:16 recordings). The root gets `.is-tall` before anything is measured, so your CSS can re-lay the product for it (stack two panes, say) and the script's targets follow. `demo/split` stacks its panes this way. **A third for squarish stages.** `data-size-square="760x760"` (or `sizeSquare: [760, 760]`) is used when .8 ≤ W/H < 1.15 (1:1 recordings, square-ish windows), and the root gets `.is-square` the same way. Without it those stages use the wide size, as before. `demo/agentic` has all three: a tiled desk (wide), and one live window beside (square) or above (tall) its run sheet. **A height that follows the frame: `auto`.** `data-size="580xauto"` (or `size: [580, 'auto']`, and the same for `sizeTall`) fixes the window's width and takes its height from the `data-tour-frame` at every layout, so the window always has the frame's shape: a full-height column on a wide page, the whole screen on a phone, any recording ratio. For products that read top to bottom (a chat, a feed, a transcript). `demo/chat` and `demo/mcp` use it. Build the product at the design size in plain CSS pixels. The engine scales the whole window, so text stays real text and stays sharp at any zoom. ### Hooks `'@name'` anywhere in a selector means `[data-tour="name"]`. Put `data-tour="…"` on the things the script points at. Pointer targets also choose the cursor: links, buttons, `role=button|tab|switch` get the hand, inputs and `data-tour-cursor="text"` get the I-beam, the rest the arrow (`data-tour-cursor="arrow|pointer|text"` overrides it). While the cursor rests on a target, that target has `.is-hover`; while it's pressed, `.is-press`. Style both so clicks read. ## The script ```js import { click, type, show, hide, set, tween, zoom, unzoom, chapter, caption, pause } from './tour.js'; export default { size: [1200, 750], // window design size (or data-size on the window) enter: [.84, .97], // where the cursor comes in from, as fractions of the window intro: 1.3, // seconds for the opening band to clear (0: no band) outro: 4.5, // seconds held on the closing frame settle: .6, // pause between the last step and the outro still: 17.4, // the moment reduced motion shows fit: [.92, .88, .5], // optional: see below steps: [ … ], }; ``` `fit: [w, h, y]` is for a stage that holds nothing but the window (a panel beside text, with no card or band over it): the window may take `w` of the stage's width and `h` of its height, centred at `y` (default .5), and push-ins aim at the middle of the frame. Without it the page layout leaves room for the card and band (`[.74, .7, .47]`). It never changes `?record`. `demo/chapters` uses it. Steps run in order on one clock. **Pointer steps** take time and the next step waits for them. **Side steps** start at the current moment and the next step starts with them, so `click('@create'), hide('@modal'), show('@toast')` hides the modal and shows the toast as the click lands. Every step takes: `at: 12.5` pin it to an absolute time · `wait: .4` start this much later · `parallel: true` (pointer steps) don't hold up the next step · `block: true` (side steps) do hold it up. ### Pointer steps | step | what happens | options (defaults) | |---|---|---| | `move(sel)` | glides there on a gentle arc, smootherstep | `dur` .9, `aim` [x, y] fractions of the target, `cursor` | | `click(sel)` | moves, presses (cursor shrinks, target gets `.is-press`), ripple | as `move` | | `dblclick(sel)` | moves, two presses, two ripples | as `move` | | `hover(sel)` | moves and rests (`.is-hover` on the target) | `dur` .9, `hold` .6 | | `type(sel, text)` | characters appear in `sel` at a human, uneven pace; `.is-caret` while typing, then blinking | `cps` 13, `rhythm` (below), `lead` (s of steady caret before the first key), `caret` (s it blinks after the last key, 1.6), `blink` (absolute time it goes) | | `stream(sel)` | each match appears in turn, like output arriving: gets `.is-in`, and `--in` 0→1 over `dur`. A match's `data-tour-wait="1.2"` adds that pause before it (a slow step) | `every` .06 s, `jitter` .5 (±50 % of `every`; 0 for an exact beat), `dur` .08 | | `drag(handle, o)` | moves to the handle, presses, then drives a value while the cursor stays on the handle | `approach` .8, `dur` 1.2, `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el` to put the property on another element), `text: [sel, v => label]`, or `onto: sel` to carry the handle itself there | | `scroll(sel, to)` | scrolls an element; `to` is px, `'50%'`, `'end'` or a selector inside it | `dur` 1.4, `offset` 16 | | `key(keys)` | key caps on screen, e.g. `key(['⌘', 'K'])` | `dur` .9, `hold` 1.4 | | `pause(s)` | a beat | | | `tap(sel)` | the same step as `click`; reads better in a touch film | as `click` | | `longpress(sel)` | moves, presses and holds; it fires (`.is-press` stays on, a ripple) after `hold`, and the finger stays down `lift` longer while the next steps start (open a context menu there) | `dur` .9, `hold` .7, `lift` .35 | | `swipe(sel, o)` | a finger flick that starts on `sel`: lands, travels `by` [dx, dy] window px speeding up, lifts while still moving. What it moves follows it 1:1, then coasts to rest over `coast` s with the speed it was let go at. `scroll: to` scrolls `sel` (or `in: sel`) to `to` (px, `'50%'`, `'end'`, a selector; `offset`); `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el`) drives a CSS variable instead (a carousel, a sheet dragged down), `follow` (.45) of it under the finger | `approach` .7, `by` [0, -220], `dur` .36, `coast` .8 (0: a slow drag that ends at rest), `settle` (when the next step starts, `coast` × .5) | `type`'s `rhythm`: unset is the even, slightly uneven pace it always had. `'human'` types like a person at a keyboard: a beat between words, a reach for symbols (`- / . : =`), a pause after punctuation, doubled letters run together, the odd hesitation. `'stream'` lands the text in chunks of 1–5 characters, the way a model's reply arrives. `stream()` is for whole lines or blocks; hide them in CSS until `.is-in` (`.line{display:none}.line.is-in{display:block}`) so they take space only once they've arrived. The cursor's path between targets is a smootherstep glide with a slight bow (direction-dependent, never a straight line) and a slightly early peak speed, like a hand. It never teleports: each move starts where the last one ended. **A finger instead of a cursor.** `pointer: 'touch'` in the script (or `data-pointer="touch"` on the root, `?pointer=touch`) swaps the arrow for a fingertip: a soft translucent dot, 44 window px, that is part of the screen, so it zooms with it. Keep it to what fits: one command, its output, one result. - **A library or project page** (`data-film="repo"`, `data-chrome="browser"`): their project as **their own docs or project site** shows it (not a copy of a code host's UI): name, README first line, the real install line in `.clr-install` (the Copy click), and the real notes of their first stable release in `.clr-notes` (Added / Changed / Fixed, as they wrote them). `data-url` is the address people would see. - **An app** (`data-film="app"`, `data-chrome="app"` or `browser` for a web app): harvest the real screen (`uv run tour/snapshot.py <url> --selector … --size 720x412 --out changelog/fragments/app.html --hook …`) or rebuild it from their view code in their tokens, then make the film do the one thing it's for: a new item, then its page. `ITEM` in `script.js` is that item's name, in the app's own vocabulary. - Other shipped things fit the same slots: a site (`browser`), a phone app (`data-chrome="phone"` with `data-size="390x844"` and a matching stage aspect), a design system's docs page, a dataset's explorer. - **Static HTML/CSS only, no app logic.** Their sample content or kit placeholders where user data would appear; never real people's data. - **Pace**: 7–11 s each, every click visibly changes something, one push-in at most (`zoom('@x', 1.3)`) then `unzoom()`, and the last frame is the result. Set `still` to that result (shown with reduced motion). ## 4. The rail and the reading You don't write the rail: `section.js` builds a row per release from the markup. Check it after filling the log: every entry is a mark on its week (Shipped in the accent), the head moves to the entry at the reading line, clicking a mark goes to its entry. On phones and tablets it's a bar across the top that shows the release being read. ## 5. Unreleased: the ending - `NEXT_LINE` in `changelog/script.js` is the line the cursor drafts: what they want to do next, with the visitor, in their own words, one line ("Working with you on …"). `next_version` in `.cln-t1` is the version it becomes. - `.cl-addr`: the email they want strangers to use, set large; GitHub; the feed; their domain. - `.cln-sub` is the second line of the draft. Keep it short and true. ## 6. Check it - The page at 1440 × 900 and on a 390-wide phone: each film plays once as it reaches the middle and shows "Play again" after; the rail follows; no sideways scroll; the Unreleased entry drafts and the address appears. - `index.html?t=6` freezes every film at 6 s. With reduced motion every film shows its `still` and the address is in. - `?record&ratio=16:9`, `ratio=1:1` and `ratio=9:16`, each with several `&t=` (`window.changelog.duration` is the length; `changelog.seek(30)` jumps there): the reading holds on Now, stops at each release, plays each film with its entry above it, and ends on Unreleased with the address in. Text must be readable in 1:1. - Nothing left that is lorem, a placeholder you meant to replace, a link to `#`, a number you can't source, or contact details they didn't agree to publish. Delete every `<span class="sf-note">`. ## 7. Hand it over: record and post End by giving the person this, with the link filled in: 1. Open **`index.html?record&ratio=16:9`** (served, e.g. `http://localhost:8000/?record&ratio=16:9`) in a browser window 1920 × 1080 if your screen allows, otherwise the largest 16:9 window you can make on a Retina display. 2. Record it with **Monet Shot**: choose the browser window, crop to the stage, park the real pointer off the window (the films draw their own cursor). It holds on Now for 1.2 s, reads the whole log once by itself and stops on the Unreleased entry with the address in. Monet Shot adds no zooms of its own, because the clicks aren't real clicks; if you'd rather place zooms on its timeline, open `?record&ratio=16:9&camera=off` so you don't get both. 3. Export H.264 MP4 and post it to X with one line and the link. **16:9** is for X and LinkedIn; `ratio=1:1` for the feed; `ratio=9:16` for stories and reels. Record each ratio separately; the page lays itself out again for each, so never crop one into another. 4. X takes MP4 (H.264, AAC) up to 2 min 20 s and 512 MB. There's no caption line: the log's own entries are set large enough to read muted, so keep the entry text short. 5. When something ships, add the entry, change Now's date, regenerate `feed.xml`, and record again: the changelog is meant to be kept.

# tour.js: the demo-film engine One engine for every StyleFeatures demo film. A template supplies a window with a product inside it and a script; the engine plays it with a fake cursor, a camera, chapter cards and captions, and drives it from a scroll, a clock, a screen recorder or a frozen `?t=`. Files: | file | what it is | edit it? | |---|---|---| | `tour.js` | the engine: step builders, `Tour`, `include()` | no, it's shared by every format | | `tour.css` | the engine's look: chromes, cursor, card, caption, keys, controls, record stage | no; restyle through its tokens | | `script.js` | this film's script | yes | | `section.html` / `section.css` | this film's band, closing frame and product | yes | | `snapshot.py` | harvests a live screen into a static fragment | no | | `export.py` | copies the whole format out as a standalone folder | no | | `AGENT.md` | the brief for the coding agent that fills it in | read it | Everything on screen is a pure function of one number, `t`, in seconds. Each frame the engine works out the product's state at `t` (classes, attributes, text, CSS variables, scroll positions), the camera, the cursor and the overlays, then writes only what changed. Nothing depends on what happened in earlier frames, so any moment renders on its own, the same way every time. ## Markup ```html
… your product, built at 1200 × 750 design pixels …
…
…
``` The engine adds the chrome, the cursor, ripples, the chapter card, the caption line, key caps, and the driver's controls. The opening band (`data-tour-band`) slides away in the first `intro` seconds; the closing frame (`data-tour-end`) gets `--in` 0→1 at the end and its own CSS decides what that looks like. The root also carries `--tour-band` (1 → 0 over the intro), `--tour-out` (0 → 1 over the outro) and `--tour-p` (0 → 1 over the whole film) for a format's own CSS. `data-tour-band="css"` stops the engine sliding the band away; the format fades or moves it from `--tour-band` instead. **A frame the format draws: `data-tour-frame`.** Put an element with `data-tour-frame` in the stage and lay it out in CSS (a phone's glass, a mat around a screenshot, a different box per ratio). The engine fits the window to it exactly, clips the camera to it (with its `border-radius`), and every zoom stays inside it: the window always covers the frame, so a push-in never shows what's around it. The outro then leaves the window where it is (use `--tour-out` to do something else). Give the frame the window's aspect ratio. `demo/phone` (the glass, beside the text or under it) and `demo/launch-note` (a mat on the page, a different box per recording ratio) use it. ### Window chromes: `data-chrome` | value | looks like | typical `data-size` | |---|---|---| | `browser` | traffic lights, back/forward, an address pill (`data-url`), share/new icons | `1200x750` | | `app` | a macOS title bar with traffic lights and a centred `data-title` | `1200x760` | | `phone` | a dark bezel, a status bar with the time and a notch | `390x844` | | `none` | just rounded corners | anything | | `terminal` | a warm charcoal window, traffic lights, a centred `data-title`; tokens `--tour-term-bg/-bar/-ink/-dim` | `780x548` | **Windows inside the window.** Any element inside the window with a `data-chrome` gets that chrome too, and a frame (`display:flex`, rounded, clipped). With `data-chrome="none"` on the outer window (made transparent in your CSS) it becomes a desk holding, say, a terminal and a browser; the camera pans between them with `zoom()` (`demo/terminal` does this). **A second design size for tall stages.** `data-size-tall="440x820"` on the window (or `sizeTall: [440, 820]` in the script) is used whenever the stage is taller than wide (W/H < .8: phones, 9:16 recordings). The root gets `.is-tall` before anything is measured, so your CSS can re-lay the product for it (stack two panes, say) and the script's targets follow. `demo/split` stacks its panes this way. **A third for squarish stages.** `data-size-square="760x760"` (or `sizeSquare: [760, 760]`) is used when .8 ≤ W/H < 1.15 (1:1 recordings, square-ish windows), and the root gets `.is-square` the same way. Without it those stages use the wide size, as before. `demo/agentic` has all three: a tiled desk (wide), and one live window beside (square) or above (tall) its run sheet. **A height that follows the frame: `auto`.** `data-size="580xauto"` (or `size: [580, 'auto']`, and the same for `sizeTall`) fixes the window's width and takes its height from the `data-tour-frame` at every layout, so the window always has the frame's shape: a full-height column on a wide page, the whole screen on a phone, any recording ratio. For products that read top to bottom (a chat, a feed, a transcript). `demo/chat` and `demo/mcp` use it. Build the product at the design size in plain CSS pixels. The engine scales the whole window, so text stays real text and stays sharp at any zoom. ### Hooks `'@name'` anywhere in a selector means `[data-tour="name"]`. Put `data-tour="…"` on the things the script points at. Pointer targets also choose the cursor: links, buttons, `role=button|tab|switch` get the hand, inputs and `data-tour-cursor="text"` get the I-beam, the rest the arrow (`data-tour-cursor="arrow|pointer|text"` overrides it). While the cursor rests on a target, that target has `.is-hover`; while it's pressed, `.is-press`. Style both so clicks read. ## The script ```js import { click, type, show, hide, set, tween, zoom, unzoom, chapter, caption, pause } from './tour.js'; export default { size: [1200, 750], // window design size (or data-size on the window) enter: [.84, .97], // where the cursor comes in from, as fractions of the window intro: 1.3, // seconds for the opening band to clear (0: no band) outro: 4.5, // seconds held on the closing frame settle: .6, // pause between the last step and the outro still: 17.4, // the moment reduced motion shows fit: [.92, .88, .5], // optional: see below steps: [ … ], }; ``` `fit: [w, h, y]` is for a stage that holds nothing but the window (a panel beside text, with no card or band over it): the window may take `w` of the stage's width and `h` of its height, centred at `y` (default .5), and push-ins aim at the middle of the frame. Without it the page layout leaves room for the card and band (`[.74, .7, .47]`). It never changes `?record`. `demo/chapters` uses it. Steps run in order on one clock. **Pointer steps** take time and the next step waits for them. **Side steps** start at the current moment and the next step starts with them, so `click('@create'), hide('@modal'), show('@toast')` hides the modal and shows the toast as the click lands. Every step takes: `at: 12.5` pin it to an absolute time · `wait: .4` start this much later · `parallel: true` (pointer steps) don't hold up the next step · `block: true` (side steps) do hold it up. ### Pointer steps | step | what happens | options (defaults) | |---|---|---| | `move(sel)` | glides there on a gentle arc, smootherstep | `dur` .9, `aim` [x, y] fractions of the target, `cursor` | | `click(sel)` | moves, presses (cursor shrinks, target gets `.is-press`), ripple | as `move` | | `dblclick(sel)` | moves, two presses, two ripples | as `move` | | `hover(sel)` | moves and rests (`.is-hover` on the target) | `dur` .9, `hold` .6 | | `type(sel, text)` | characters appear in `sel` at a human, uneven pace; `.is-caret` while typing, then blinking | `cps` 13, `rhythm` (below), `lead` (s of steady caret before the first key), `caret` (s it blinks after the last key, 1.6), `blink` (absolute time it goes) | | `stream(sel)` | each match appears in turn, like output arriving: gets `.is-in`, and `--in` 0→1 over `dur`. A match's `data-tour-wait="1.2"` adds that pause before it (a slow step) | `every` .06 s, `jitter` .5 (±50 % of `every`; 0 for an exact beat), `dur` .08 | | `drag(handle, o)` | moves to the handle, presses, then drives a value while the cursor stays on the handle | `approach` .8, `dur` 1.2, `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el` to put the property on another element), `text: [sel, v => label]`, or `onto: sel` to carry the handle itself there | | `scroll(sel, to)` | scrolls an element; `to` is px, `'50%'`, `'end'` or a selector inside it | `dur` 1.4, `offset` 16 | | `key(keys)` | key caps on screen, e.g. `key(['⌘', 'K'])` | `dur` .9, `hold` 1.4 | | `pause(s)` | a beat | | | `tap(sel)` | the same step as `click`; reads better in a touch film | as `click` | | `longpress(sel)` | moves, presses and holds; it fires (`.is-press` stays on, a ripple) after `hold`, and the finger stays down `lift` longer while the next steps start (open a context menu there) | `dur` .9, `hold` .7, `lift` .35 | | `swipe(sel, o)` | a finger flick that starts on `sel`: lands, travels `by` [dx, dy] window px speeding up, lifts while still moving. What it moves follows it 1:1, then coasts to rest over `coast` s with the speed it was let go at. `scroll: to` scrolls `sel` (or `in: sel`) to `to` (px, `'50%'`, `'end'`, a selector; `offset`); `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el`) drives a CSS variable instead (a carousel, a sheet dragged down), `follow` (.45) of it under the finger | `approach` .7, `by` [0, -220], `dur` .36, `coast` .8 (0: a slow drag that ends at rest), `settle` (when the next step starts, `coast` × .5) | `type`'s `rhythm`: unset is the even, slightly uneven pace it always had. `'human'` types like a person at a keyboard: a beat between words, a reach for symbols (`- / . : =`), a pause after punctuation, doubled letters run together, the odd hesitation. `'stream'` lands the text in chunks of 1–5 characters, the way a model's reply arrives. `stream()` is for whole lines or blocks; hide them in CSS until `.is-in` (`.line{display:none}.line.is-in{display:block}`) so they take space only once they've arrived. The cursor's path between targets is a smootherstep glide with a slight bow (direction-dependent, never a straight line) and a slightly early peak speed, like a hand. It never teleports: each move starts where the last one ended. **A finger instead of a cursor.** `pointer: 'touch'` in the script (or `data-pointer="touch"` on the root, `?pointer=touch`) swaps the arrow for a fingertip: a soft translucent dot, 44 window px, that is part of the screen, so it zooms with it. It is unseen between touches (a hand travelling isn't on the glass); a shadow gathers for a fifth of a second before contact, the dot flattens and darkens while pressed (`.is-down` on `.tour-cur`), and lifts away. `drag` and `swipe` carry it across the glass. Give each touch a beat: the `dur` before it is the hand travelling. Restyle the dot with `--tour-touch` / `--tour-touch-down`. `demo/phone` is the worked example. **More than one pointer.** Any pointer step with `by: 'agent'` moves a second cursor on its own track (any name works; steps without `by` move the usual one, `'main'`). Describe each in the script: ```js pointers: { main: { label: 'You', idle: 1.4 }, // a tag on the person's cursor; it fades after 1.4 s still agent: { label: 'Agent', look: 'agent', bow: .2, enter: [.33, .2] }, }, steps: [ click('@search', { by: 'agent', tag: 'search_code' }), …, click('@approve', { from: [.99, 1.03] }) ] ``` A second pointer is an arrow in `--tour-agent` (look `'agent'`) with a label tag beside it; `tag` on a step adds a word to that label from then on (the tool it's using, "waiting for you"). `bow` scales the curve of its path (0 is a straight, machine-like line), `enter` is where it first appears, `shapes: true` lets it take the hand and I-beam too. `idle: s` fades a pointer out once it has been still that long and back in when it next moves; `from: [x, y]` (fractions of the window) on a step starts that move there instead, so a hand can come back in from off the edge. Each pointer's clicks ripple in its own colour (`.tour-ring[data-who]`), and `.tour-cur[data-who="…"]` lets a page hide one (`demo/agentic` hides the person's cursor on the live page, where the visitor is the person). Touch mode (`pointer: 'touch'`) applies to the main pointer only. ### Side steps | step | what happens | options | |---|---|---| | `show(sel)` / `hide(sel)` | tweens `--in` to 1 / 0 on every match; your CSS uses `opacity: var(--in)` etc. | `dur` .35 / .28, `stagger` | | `set(sel, changes)` | instant: `{class: '+on -off'}`, `{text: 'Copied'}`, `{'--x': 2}`, `{'data-view': 'room'}`, `{attr: null}` removes | | | `tween(sel, prop, from, to)` | animates a CSS variable, `'text'` (with `fmt`) or `'scrollTop'` | `dur` .45, `fmt`, `stagger` | | `zoom(sel, z)` | camera pushes in on the target. `z` a number, or `'fit'` to frame the element at `fill` of the frame | `dur` 1.3, `fill` .66 (or `[wide, stacked]`, e.g. `[.76, .96]`: tighter on 1:1 and phones, where the window is small), `aim`, `max` 2.6 (the most a `'fit'` may push in: raise it for a big window such as a whole board), `arc` 0 (0–1: pull back by that share mid-flight and push in again, so a long pan reads as a camera crossing; `demo/canvas`) | | `unzoom()` | camera back to the whole window | `dur` 1.3 | | `chapter(n, title, line)` | the card: `'02 / 05'`, a title with one `` word, one line; until the next chapter | `until` | | `caption(text)` | the caption line, until the next caption | `dur` 4 | | `mark(name)` | nothing on screen: a named moment. `tour.api.marks` lists them in order (`{ t, name }`) and `marks[name]` is that moment's time, so a page can seek to one or stop at the next (`demo/chat`'s beats, `demo/mcp`'s tabs) | | `show`, `hide` and `tween` take `ease`: `'out'` (decelerate), `'ios'` (a critically damped spring, UIKit's pushes and sheets), `'spring'` (overshoots by about 3 %), `'linear'`, or any `(t) => t` function. The default is smootherstep. The curves are exported as `eases`. `data-tour-follow` on a scrolling element (a terminal, a chat thread, a log) keeps its newest content in view every frame, so lines that `stream()` in push the old ones up. `data-tour-grow` on an element that should take height as it arrives (a message in a thread, a folded panel): the engine measures its natural height into `--h` (design px, innermost first, before targets are measured, and again on every relayout), so your CSS can open it with `--in` and let go once it's in: `max-height: max(calc(var(--in) * var(--h)), calc((var(--in) - .999) * 1e7px))`. Rows arrive smoothly and may change size afterwards. `../_chat/chat.css` is the worked example. Elements that `show()` controls should start hidden in CSS (`--in: 0`). Anything the script changes is reset when you seek backwards, because every value is recomputed from `t`. ### The camera `zoom` pushes in on a point and keeps the window filling the frame: it borrows Monet Shot's fit clamp, so a push-in never pans past the window's edge (the window is either wholly inside the frame or covers it). Zoom levels move on a log scale, so in and out feel even. Numbers are multiplied by 1.15 on portrait stages, where the window is small (not inside a `data-tour-frame`, which the window always fills). `?camera=off` turns all push-ins off. On stacked stages (1:1, 9:16, phones) the cursor fades out rather than being drawn outside the window's frame. ### Measuring Targets are measured in the window's own pixels, against the product as it is at the moment each step happens (so a button inside a modal that opens two steps earlier is measured with the modal open), and measured again whenever the layout can change: fonts loading, the stage resizing, your CSS. Edit the product freely; the script follows. ## The card and caption keep out of the way The chapter card and the caption never sit on what the tour is doing. Each frame the engine checks the cursor (or fingertip) and any text being typed (`type`) or streamed in (`stream`), with its last second after. If the card would cover it, the card slides to the other side of the stage; if both sides are busy it steps out, and it comes home once the spot has been clear for .8 s. The caption lifts to the top. Outside `?record` the card carries a × that hides the cards for the rest of the visit; recordings have none. Nothing to configure. In stacked layouts (phones, 9:16) the card already sits under the window, so nothing moves. ## Drivers | driver | how | when | |---|---|---| | `scroll` (default) | `data-driver="scroll"`. The section gets tall, the stage pins, scroll maps to `t`. The gate starts an auto-play drift at real speed. With `data-lock` (default on) wheel, touch and keys can't skip the film while it drifts; the Auto-play switch is the way out. A film at the very top of the page holds the page still until the first click, tap or key. | the opening of a launch page, Monet Shot style | | `play` | `data-driver="play"`. A 100svh stage with a play button, a scrubber with chapter ticks and a timecode. Space or K plays, arrows step 3 s. | a film in the middle of a page | | `manual` | `data-driver="manual"` (or `new Tour(root, script, { driver: 'manual' })`). No gate, controls or scroll handling: it draws `t = 0` and waits. The page drives it with the instance's `play()`, `pause()`, `render(t)`, `load(script)` (or `tour.api`), and may set `tour.onFrame = (t) => …`, called after every frame. `play()` dispatches `tour:end` on the root when it reaches the end. | a format with its own idea of when to play: `demo/chapters` (one film per chapter, played as you reach it), `demo/playground` | | `?t=12.5` | freezes that moment, any driver. Use it to check stills. | checking | | loop | `data-loop` on the root, `loop: true` in the script or `?loop`: the `play` driver starts again at the end, fading the window through the seam. Never in `?record`, which plays once. `begin()` (or `tour.api.begin()`) starts it from code, e.g. when it scrolls into view. | a short feature loop: `demo/launch-note` | | reduced motion | shows `still` with the camera off and the card on: the whole window, a sensible frame | always on | | `?record` | see below | recording | `data-music="audio/track.mp3"` on the root starts a loop with a fade at the gate. `data-captions`: `record` (default: only in `?record`), `always`, `off`. `data-cursor="off"` hides the cursor; `data-cursor-look="light"` gives a white arrow. ## Recording: `?record` ``` index.html?record&ratio=16:9 16:9, 1:1 or 9:16, centred in the browser window &hold=1.2 seconds held on the first frame before it plays (default 1.2) &camera=off no push-ins (see below) &captions=off no caption line &t=12.5 a frozen frame of the recording, for checking ``` It renders only the stage, at the largest box of that ratio that fits the window, on near-black, with no page, notes, spec card, gate or controls, and sizes the overlays to the stage. The film may sit anywhere in the page, inside another section: everything that isn't the film or one of its ancestors is hidden. It holds the first frame (the title band), plays once from 0 and stops on the closing frame. Captions are on, because X autoplays muted. Record it with **Monet Shot**: pick the browser window, crop to the stage, and export. Two things to know: - Monet Shot zooms on **real** clicks. The tour's clicks are drawn, not real, so Monet Shot sees none and adds no zooms of its own. The tour's camera therefore stays **on** by default. If you would rather place zooms yourself on Monet Shot's timeline, use `&camera=off` and you won't get double zooms. - Monet Shot draws its own cursor from the real pointer. Park the real pointer off the recorded window (or set Monet Shot's cursor to hidden) so only the tour's cursor shows. From script: `window.tour` has `seek(t)`, `play()`, `pause()`, `load(script)`, `t`, `duration`, `chapters` and `ready` (a promise that resolves once fonts are in and everything is measured). The root gets a `tour:end` event whenever `play()` reaches the end (any driver). **Several tours in one recorded frame.** A format whose recording is more than one film (two windows racing in `demo/versus`, a whole slide deck in `demo/deck`) makes its own element the record stage and drives the tours itself: ```js import { Tour, recordStage } from './tour.js'; const box = q.has('record') ? recordStage(root) : null; // root becomes the ratio's box, centred on near-black, the rest hidden const a = new Tour(filmA, scriptA, { driver: 'manual', record: 'page' }); // no record stage or auto-play of its own a.render(t); // the page decides t, every frame ``` `recordStage(el)` does for `el` what `?record` does for a single film (the `tour-record` and `sf-clean` classes, `--rw`/`--rh` from `&ratio=`, kept current on resize) and returns `{ w, h, ratio }`. `{ record: 'page' }` on a Tour means: in `?record` stay on the manual driver and let the page play it (captions follow `captions` as usual). Without `?record` it changes nothing. ``` `snapshot.py` captures an element of a running page with all its computed styles into a scoped, static fragment (`uv run tour/snapshot.py --help`). `--mobile` captures a mobile web build as a phone sees it (mobile viewport, touch, an iPhone user agent). `examples/harvest/` (in the StyleFeatures repo) is a working example: a live pricing page captured in two states and clicked through. ## Making another format Two more formats are built this way, as worked examples: `../terminal/` (a desk with a terminal and a browser, typed commands, streamed output, `ansi.py` for capturing a CLI's real output) and `../split/` (input and output panes that stack on phones).
